entries.title: GOP Governor Candidate Plans to Ask for ICE Agents at Polling Places
entries.summary: Bobby Charles is running against Democrat Hannah Pingree in Maine.
entries.content:
Maine gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles said he plans to ask White House border czar Tom Homan to send U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to Maine polling stations this election season.

If Charles succeeds, the move could validate long-held fears by many in the Democratic Party that President Donald Trump could use immigration agents to intimidate voters or assist in potential efforts to tamper with election results.

“I’m going to ask Tom — three or four weeks before the election, maybe three — I’m going to make an appeal for ICE and marshals to be at our voting booths,” Charles said last week in an audio recording obtained and reported first by the Bangor Daily News Wednesday. “Do you think the illegals who are being paid money are going to like that?”

The Republican nominee’s comments come as the state is still grappling with the death of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Columbian national who was shot and killed by ICE on July 13 in Biddeford, Maine. Durán Guerrero was not the intended target of the operation, but his killing sparked heated protests against federal immigration enforcement in the state.

Charles called Homan a “friend” and added that the pair “used to be on Fox [News] all the time together” at a gathering with Maine Young Republicans on Aug. 20. It appears to be the first time a midterm candidate said they plan to ask the federal government to deploy immigration agents to polling locations.

The comment is in line with President Donald Trump’s push to crack down on noncitizen voting — though there is little evidence to support the idea that noncitizens are voting in large numbers or that massive enforcement efforts would have stopped the few who have been caught.

Deploying ICE agents to polling locations may also be illegal under federal statutes that prohibit federal officials from interfering with elections and intimidating voters. Federal law enforcement officials or “armed men” are also prohibited where an “election is held.”

ICE referred NOTUS to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s comments during his confirmation hearing, where he said “the only reason why my officers would be there is if there was a specific threat for them to be there, not for intimidation.”

The U.S. Marshals Service did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Charles’ campaign did not dispute the remark when reached by Bangor Daily News, but added that the “point is that Bobby will do everything legally possible to prevent illegal voting in Maine.”

Democrats quickly voiced their opposition to Charles’ plan, with Devon Murphy-Anderson, Maine’s Democratic Party executive director, calling the push for ICE at Maine’s polling locations “not only deeply alarming — it is likely illegal.”

Maine’s Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, a Democrat who is tasked with overseeing the elections process, affirmed that federal law enforcement officials are “prohibited from being at the polls on Election Day.”

“Bobby Charles can call whoever he wants, but he can’t change the Constitution or the law,” Bellows told the Bangor Daily News.

Some in Trump’s inner circle have floated sending ICE agents to the polls, but the administration has said they will not pursue the enforcement efforts.

Trump’s former chief strategist Steve Bannon said earlier this year that deploying ICE agents to U.S. airports would be a “perfect training for the fall of 2026,” but the Department of Homeland Security told election officials “there will be no ICE presence at polling locations for this election” in a virtual meeting in February.

Charles is set to face Pingree in November. The Republican faces an uphill climb in the race, which is rated “solid D” by Cook Political Report. Vice President JD Vance backed Charles earlier this week at a rally in Maine, but Trump has yet to formally back the Republican candidate.

“My opponent is on the internet pretending he is no longer a proxy for Donald Trump, and meanwhile he is begging Trump’s ICE to come interfere with our free and fair elections,” Pingree told NOTUS. “I think that conduct speaks for itself and I trust the Maine people to see it for what it is.”

Democrats are heading into the election with the advantage, and Charles has made efforts to distance himself from the president. At a campaign event last week, the Republican told voters he does not know Trump.

“But, I will work with him,” Charles said. “I will also stand up against him if he opposes something Maine needs.”

entries.title: Federal Judge Strikes Down Texas Drag Show Ban: ‘Just Don’t Go’
entries.summary: Under the law, businesses that hosted drag shows would have received civil penalties while performers could have been criminally penalized.
entries.content:
A federal judge in Texas struck down a state ban on drag performances, deeming it an unconstitutional restriction on free speech, according to a court order filed this week.

The Tuesday ruling by U.S. District Judge David Hittner bars Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is currently running for Senate, from enforcing a law signed by Gov. Greg Abbott in 2023 that targeted “sexually oriented” performances in front of minors. Abbott touted the law as a ban on public drag shows — an activity increasingly targeted by right-wing figures in recent years.

Under Texas’ law, businesses that hosted drag shows would receive civil penalties while performers would be criminally penalized.

Hittner, a Reagan appointee, also denied Paxton’s motion for a new trial on the case. He signed off his ruling with a suggestion for “those who find such activities as described in this case offensive.”

“The solution is relatively simple ... just don't go,” Hittner wrote.

Paxton wrote on X that Hittner’s ruling was a “profoundly flawed decision that endangers our children and is an affront to Texas values.” He said he would appeal the decision and “continue to fight to protect our kids.”

Hittner initially deemed the case unconstitutional in 2023. The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals later returned the case to him with instructions to reevaluate a select number of details. Hittner reaffirmed his original decision Tuesday, writing that the nature of “sexually oriented" performances was too broad.

Hittner added that there were “‘erotic’ elements in countless popular performances” that critics could say violate state law, including “Elvis's signature hip gyrations,” Dolly Parton’s status as a “voluptuous sex symbol because of her big hair, flamboyant clothes and breast exposure” or Miley Cyrus “‘twerking’ on stage during a live performance at the 2013 MTV Video Music Awards.”

Drag performer Brigitte Bandit, a plaintiff in the lawsuit, celebrated Hittner’s ruling on Instagram Tuesday, saying, “Drag is free speech, bitch.”

entries.title: Josh Shapiro and RFK Jr. Trade Barbs Over Deadly Measles Outbreak
entries.summary: Kennedy questioned if the two deaths in Pennsylvania “actually happened.”
entries.content:
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. have clashed publicly after two unvaccinated residents in the state died from measles, the first such deaths in Pennsylvania in decades.

At a news conference Tuesday, Shapiro arrived late, saying he was on a phone call with Kennedy — a call he described as “blunt.”

Shapiro, a Democrat, said he “made very clear that [Kennedy’s] actions and the rhetoric that’s coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America, particularly right here in Pennsylvania.”

“There's real-life consequences to spreading misinformation,” the governor added. “There’s real-life consequences to scaring people and not relying on actual doctors, actual medical professionals, to provide unbiased information to parents so that we can make reasonable decisions for our kids.”

Kennedy said Wednesday that Shapiro’s office was unwilling to provide workers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention with any details about the deaths. He also praised how the U.S. was handling the recent increase in measles cases.

Kennedy also went as far as questioning if the deaths in Lancaster County even happened.

“‘The press is all covering this [as] if those measles deaths actually happened, and nobody is doing any critical inquiry to find out,” he said. “We’re trying to find out whether those deaths actually happened, and we can’t figure that out.”

In Pennsylvania alone, 393 measles cases in 28 counties have been confirmed this year; 86 of those cases came in the past week. Shapiro said every confirmed case has occurred in people who are not fully vaccinated.

Kennedy also said Wednesday that Shapiro admitted to him during the Tuesday phone call that the drop in vaccinations took place while Joe Biden was president — a point Kennedy also made on X.

Shapiro denied this, also in a post on X, stating that Kennedy’s statements are “inaccurate and misleading and he is making claims that have been debunked repeatedly by actual scientists and doctors.”

“Kennedy’s actions to dismantle public health agencies and his language that undermines confidence in vetted medical guidance are contributing to these kinds of outbreaks,” Shapiro wrote. “Just a few years ago, Secretary Kennedy was in Lancaster downplaying the severity of measles and saying that the cure was ‘chicken soup and vitamin A.'"

entries.title: AOC Officially Rejoins DSA as 2028 Speculation Heats Up
entries.summary: DSA said the “ongoing discussions” about 2028 prompted them to confirm the congresswoman’s affiliation with the organization.
entries.content:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has officially rejoined the Democratic Socialists of America this month after her membership expired seven years ago.

The New York Democrat, who first signed up for an annual membership in 2018, is the most prominent politician affiliated with the organization despite having let her official affiliation lapse for seven years.

DSA-linked candidates have amassed a string of wins this primary season, knocking off some long-standing Democratic incumbents in the process — sometimes to the chagrin of moderate lawmakers on the left. But as Ocasio-Cortez leads some recent polling among potential Democratic presidential candidates, her decision to reestablish membership with the DSA could further boost the progressive political organization’s relevance beyond this midterms cycle.

“Democratic Socialists of America confirms Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is a member in good standing of our organization, having recently rejoined in August 2026,” DSA wrote in a statement shared with City & State New York. “Previously, the representative joined DSA in 2018 with a one-year membership, which DSA’s national leadership recently noticed had lapsed, in 2019. She has since renewed her membership as of this month.”

Some DSA members have been considering what putting up a presidential candidate in 2028 could look like, The Washington Post reported this month, and Ocasio-Cortez is currently one of their best chances at reaching the country’s highest office.

“While it is atypical for DSA to address the membership status of individuals, ongoing discussions about the 2028 presidential campaign have prompted this release,” the organization said.

DSA has referred to Ocasio-Cortez as a “member” several times in the past seven years, despite her lapsed membership.

The congresswoman did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ocasio-Cortez won her first U.S. House race in 2018 by toppling 10-term incumbent Joe Crowley in the Democratic primary for New York’s 14th Congressional District. Although she appears to have only been an official card-carrying member of the DSA for one year, her four terms in the House spurred a movement for other congressional hopefuls hoping to upset candidates they considered to be part of the Democratic establishment.

DSA-endorsed nominees like Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York and Melat Kiros in Colorado clinched breakthrough victories in their primaries this year, while other candidates linked to the DSA have also seen some success. And New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s DSA-backed victory last fall further elevated the organization’s national profile, though the progressive politician tried to distinguish his platform from some of the DSA’s national policy goals while on the campaign trail.

Ocasio-Cortez has at times endured a rocky relationship with the organization. DSA withdrew, then conditionally reinstated, their support for the congresswoman’s 2024 U.S. House campaign, citing her vote for a resolution that equated the “denial of Israel’s right to exist” as a form of antisemitism.

At a private DSA meeting earlier this year, Ocasio-Cortez said she would not authorize any military aid to Israel and cited her record of voting “no” on the issue.

“The Israeli government should be able to finance their own weapons if they seek to arm themselves,” Ocasio-Cortez said, City & State New York reported in April.

entries.title: Pentagon Claims Hegseth’s Afghanistan Withdrawal Probe Found ‘Hidden’ Files
entries.summary: Officials would not say what the files contained, where exactly they were found or whether the federal government intended to make them public
entries.content:
The chairman of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s panel reviewing the deadly 2021 withdrawal from Afghanistan claimed on Wednesday it found “hidden” documents about the military operation in a safe.

Sean Parnell, who also serves as the Pentagon’s spokesperson, made the statement in a video tribute on the fifth anniversary of Abbey Gate, a terror attack at the Kabul airport that killed 13 U.S. service members. Parnell did not share the contents of the files, which he pitched as a bombshell discovery.

Parnell said the “highly relevant, classified documents” consisted of material “that should have been disclosed.” He said the documents had been “stashed and hidden away in safes where they would not be found.”

“And after the team reviewed these documents, it became clear why someone tried to hide them,” he said, without providing any further detail.

The Pentagon did not immediately return a request for comment on the contents of the documents, where exactly they were found and if the federal government intended to make them public.

The message came hours before Hegseth held an event recognizing Marines with upgraded valor awards for their contributions to the operation. Parnell said during a short address that the service members should have received the valor awards in the past but didn’t because “the record did not fully reflect” their actions. The change came after the review panel’s probe progressed, Parnell said.

Hegseth tasked Parnell in May 2025 with leading the Afghanistan Withdrawal Special Review Panel, a new federal probe into the military operation that occurred under the Biden administration.

Congressional Republicans launched a separate probe into the operation in 2023, which resulted in a 200-page report released in September 2024 that accused the Biden administration of “creating an unsafe environment” that exposed federal government personnel to “lethal threats.” The report largely left out the role of President Donald Trump’s first administration in the lead-up to the withdrawal.

Parnell said in April that the new probe would be more comprehensive than the Republican-led effort that was commissioned under former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin. Parnell argued the first probe was “over-classified at the highest levels, which effectively kept the most critical and relevant information from public scrutiny.”

Parnell said his investigation had so far completed interviews with military figures involved in the planning and execution of the withdrawal, as well as reviewed 9 million documents.

It’s unclear when the panel’s findings will be made public.

entries.title: The Commanders Have Their Offensive Issues Exposed in Joint Practice
entries.summary: With Week 1 fast approaching, Washington looked a step behind the Ravens in Baltimore.
entries.content:
If nothing else, Jayden Daniels is an optimist.

After another shaky performance by Washington’s offense, this time in a joint practice in Baltimore, Daniels appeared frustrated with how his unit looked less than a month away from the start of the season.

In his post-practice press conference, the quarterback stared off into the distance in stretches, gathering his thoughts. He provided what felt like sarcastic laughs when discussing the team’s injury issues and the offensive line. But, when asked about his general concerns following a day of mistakes, Daniels kept everything in perspective.

“You just overall have to keep building and keep growing,” he said after the joint practice session with the Ravens. “You’re not winning a Super Bowl right now. You’re not playing for a Super Bowl right now.”

He’s right. The Super Bowl isn’t for another 172 days. Week 18 is 137 days out. Even Week 1 is still 18 days away. The Commanders, in theory, have a lot of time to right the ship. But that doesn’t change what was obvious Wednesday: Washington’s offense will be incapable of moving the ball down the field this season if the offensive line doesn’t improve.

In Baltimore, the group had trouble keeping Ravens out of the backfield. The running backs, who averaged a paltry 2.1 yards per carry against the Lions last week, struggled to find running room. And when rookie Robert Henry Jr. did find space on one play, he fumbled the ball away at the end of his run.

On passing plays, Daniels was constantly forced to move around the pocket or scramble. Rookie center Matt Gulbin, taking the first-team snaps that had previously gone to Julian Good-Jones, didn’t exactly seize the opportunity. On one of the first plays during 11-on-11 drills, he was pushed into the running back, ending the play before it had a chance to start. Later, Gulbin snapped a ball too low in shotgun, leading to a rushed throw and an interception. But Daniels seemed unfazed by the uncertainty at center.

“Doing my job with the guys that I have, Matt and Julian,” Daniels said. “They’re doing a great job. It’s been like that for a majority of camp, so you won’t see me complaining.”

At other times in 11-on-11, there were notable missed blocks by right tackle Josh Conerly Jr. and receiver Jaylin Lane.

“I feel like we were just out of sync a little bit with our combos,” Conerly said. “There were some guys next to each other that haven’t worked next to each other at all this whole camp, but we made it work, and we got going eventually.”

It wasn’t all bad: Running back Kaytron Allen continued to impress and Daniels found Terry McLaurin multiple times during the first period of 11-on-11 drills against the Ravens’ starting defense. During 45-second drills at the end of practice, Daniels — fading backward — found Antonio Williams more alone than Macaulay Culkin and hit him for a touchdown.

The defense fared better. Facing the Ravens’ starting offense, pass coverage forced Lamar Jackson to have to check down to his running backs on multiple occasions. Linebacker Dorance Armstrong and defensive tackle Javon Kinlaw stuffed Derrick Henry on back-to-back plays. Cornerback Amik Robertson picked off Jackson in the end zone during the Ravens’ 45-second drill.

But due to injuries on the front seven — defensive tackle Daron Payne and linebackers Odafe Oweh and K’Lavon Chaisson were all out — there was virtually no pass rush. It made the rest of the defense, which mostly sat back in zone coverage, susceptible in the middle of the field. At one point, Jackson found Devontez Walker on a deep route for a 70-plus-yard touchdown.

Washington will have another shot at the Ravens in its third and final preseason game Friday night. But the Commanders are running out of time to fix their issues before Week 1. At the very least, Daniels does not seem to be alone in his positive attitude.

“There's so much good shit that happened today from receivers hitting their marks, to Jayden doing what he does, O-line communicating, running off the ball. There's so much good stuff that you take away from the same day,” left tackle Brandon Coleman said.

“That's what practice is. There's good stuff, there's bad stuff, and you always want to correct the bad stuff because the good stuff is the expectation.”

entries.title: Raskin Targets Jeanine Pirro and Other Prosecutors in Misconduct Probe
entries.summary: The Maryland Democrat is looking at instances of Justice Department attorneys misleading judges.
entries.content:
U.S. attorneys in five districts have become the latest targets of House Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin’s congressional investigation into prosecutorial misconduct, which could gain steam if Democrats retake the majority next Congress.

Letters delivered Wednesday to the top federal prosecutors in the District of Columbia, Minnesota, New Jersey, Rhode Island and the Northern District of Illinois warned those offices that Democrats on the Judiciary Committee are looking at instances of Justice Department attorneys misleading judges.

Among the examples that investigators are probing: faulty subpoenas served on a Rhode Island hospital that provides gender-affirming care, and the way Illinois federal prosecutors broke grand jury rules to obtain an indictment against anti-ICE protesters only to later drop the case and try to cover up debacle by redacting transcripts.

Each letter cited what Raskin, a Democrat from Maryland, called the “appalling breakdown of prosecutorial standards and ethics taking place in your jurisdiction.” And they said that House Judiciary Committee investigators are trying to determine which officials made decisions that led to federal judges expressing concern about misconduct by line prosecutors.

“The Committee is investigating DOJ’s — and specifically your office’s — pattern of misleading the judicial branch, and by extension, the American people,” Raskin wrote.

“We also seek information as to whether attorneys in your office who questioned or rejected illegal orders have been disciplined or otherwise retaliated against by DOJ or the Trump administration,” the letters say.

Last month, Raskin demanded answers from Attorney General Todd Blanche about the incidents, but he says he never heard back. Raskin gave the five U.S. attorneys until Sept. 9 to respond.

The probe touches on what have become more frequent accusations of wrongdoing against federal prosecutors during the second Trump administration. As cited in the letter to Blanche, congressional investigators have shown heightened interest in one episode early in the Trump administration.

A prosecutor-turned-whistleblower alleged that Emil Bove — a Trump lawyer who briefly served as a top DOJ official before becoming an appellate federal judge — instructed DOJ lawyers during a March 2025 operation to take a “fuck you” approach and ignore any judge who stands in the way of rushed deportation flights.

Since then, federal judges have repeatedly criticized federal prosecutors for withholding evidence from the courts, failing to follow their orders and even deliberately misinterpreting their judicial commands.

In Minnesota earlier this summer, U.S. District Judge Patrick Schiltz blocked the Trump administration’s subpoenas against Gov. Tim Walz over the state’s immigrant sanctuary policies. He reminded federal prosecutors that “initiating a criminal investigation in order to harass political opponents or to coerce them into taking official action … is a blatantly unlawful and unethical use [of] the grand-jury process.”

And in Washington, D.C., things came to a head during the fight over President Donald Trump’s decision to tear down the White House’s East Wing. U.S. District Judge Richard Leon sided with the National Trust for Historic Preservation and ordered an immediate halt to the construction of Trump’s ballroom while leaving a narrow exception for any national security measures — only to have the White House use that as a green light for the whole project.

Leon had to issue a follow-up order two weeks later on April 16 in which he called out the federal government for trying to “turn this exception on its head.”

“That is neither a reasonable nor a correct reading of my order!” he wrote, exclamation points included. “It is, to say the least, incredible, if not disingenuous, that defendants now argue that my order does not stop ballroom construction because of the safety-and-security exception!”

Raskin’s letters were sent to Pirro in D.C.; Daniel Rosen in Minnesota; Robert Frazer in New Jersey; Andrew Boutros in the Northern District of Illinois; and Charles Calenda, who is technically the highest-ranking prosecutor in Rhode Island since his term as interim U.S. attorney expired and he was made the office’s “first assistant” to keep him in the role despite a lack of Senate approval. The letters were also sent to the DOJ’s inspector general.

The letters cite a rapid erosion in the past 18 months of the “presumption of regularity,” a legal doctrine that gives the executive branch an advantage in court when judges simply assume that government officials have done their job properly and acted within normal bounds.

That presumption is now increasingly in question, with dozens of judges across the country remarking about the way prosecutors have violated that trust by skirting the rules. The violations have become so frequent that the legal blog Just Security has updated its study on the subject four times since September, tracking the sharp rise of instances in which the government has outright ignored orders or judges have expressed distrust of government representations in court.

“Some of that misconduct is unintentional, but in many cases federal judges, including Trump appointees, have found the administration's misconduct was wilful and flagrant,” Ryan Goodman, Just Security’s co-editor-in-chief, told NOTUS.

Goodman said judges “from across the ideological spectrum have explicitly suggested that the Department of Justice has forfeited the usual presumption of regularity.”

Norm Eisen, a former ambassador who has litigated nearly 300 cases against the Trump administration, said the growing number of instances in which judges and grand juries reject DOJ attempts to criminally indict Trump’s enemies as “politically tainted decision-making” is indicative of a general awakening to the new norm.

“There’s a new legal doctrine. It’s the presumption of irregularity. And it applies when the White House intrudes on the prerogatives of independence of U.S. attorneys that have guided our nation throughout the modern era,” Eisen told NOTUS.

“What could be worse than knowingly charging innocent people because the head of the U.S. government commands it? That’s not American. That is something out of an authoritarian nightmare,” he said.

There’s some disagreement about the degree to which the Trump administration’s lawyers have gone rogue.

A conservative-tilted panel of the 9th Circuit earlier this month reversed a trial court’s decision to block an administrative subpoena the DOJ used to target QueerDoc, which bills itself as the “trans online doctor’s office.”

In October last year, U.S. District Judge Jamal Whitehead wrote that “when a federal agency issues a subpoena not to investigate legal violations but to intimidate and coerce providers into abandoning lawful medical care, it exceeds its legitimate authority and abuses the judicial process.”

In reversing the decision, U.S. Appeals Judge Carlos Bea wrote that Whitehead “improperly disregarded the presumption of regularity.”

Meanwhile, others have been caught trying to use the Trump administration’s misbehavior in court as an excuse to cast doubt on all kinds of regulatory enforcement. When the Association of American Railroads tried to push back on a 2024 safety rule that requires more than one crew member on a train, judges on the 11th Circuit Court of Appeals rejected an attempt to cast aspersions on the law as some kind of political ploy.

“Whatever stress the presumption of regularity may be under today, AAR petitioners need more than speculation and innuendo to overcome it,” Judge Robin Rosenbaum wrote last week.

Raskin’s letter seeks to expose to what degree, if any, the White House has exerted influence on the everyday affairs at regional U.S. attorneys offices. It warned the offices to preserve all records — including encrypted text messages, like those on Signal or WhatsApp — and demanded that they turn over any communications between the White House and DOJ leadership, as well as orders from DOJ brass to line prosecutors.

entries.title: What Trump’s ‘Gulf of America’ Tells Us About ‘Lake America’
entries.summary: Paths to success and pitfalls abound as the president threatens to rename another international body of water.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump has threatened to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” as the United States and Canada hurtle headlong into a trade war.

So, can Trump really do that?

Yes, in short.

But as last year’s Gulf of Mexico/Gulf of America brouhaha indicates, when a U.S. president attempts to unilaterally rename a large body of water that touches multiple nations, internal and external drama ensues.

That was particularly evident from a tranche of government records NOTUS obtained last year detailing federal government wrangling and arguments over the gulf.

Here’s what to know about Trump, Lake Ontario and nomenclatural considerations:

How Would Trump Change Lake Ontario’s Name?

The U.S. Board on Geographic Names, a multi-agency federal body, is tasked with “maintaining uniform geographic name usage throughout the federal government.” The U.S. Geological Survey, which is part of the Interior Department, serves as a lead agency for coordinating renaming requests. Traditionally, name-change requests are subject to a process of review and deliberation that could take months or years.

Trump upended geographic and geological naming conventions when he declared he’d rename the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America” upon his second inauguration.

Matters moved quickly: Trump signed an executive order on Jan. 20, 2025, that mandated the “Gulf of America” change. On Feb. 9, 2025, Trump declared “Gulf of America Day” in the United States — and also suggested Canada should become the United States’ 51st state.

The “Gulf of America” edict caused some internal tumult and logistical hiccups within federal agencies. But officials instituted a de facto media blackout over the process, little resistance emerged, and Trump ultimately got his way, particularly when the federal government’s Geographic Names Information System made the official switch.

To change Lake Ontario’s name, Trump would likely employ a similar executive order and bureaucratic process.

Congress could also pass a law codifying such a name change.

Would Americans be Forced to Call It ‘Lake America’?

Not necessarily, even if Trump tried to enforce naming doctrine. An applicable legal ruling came in April 2025, when a federal court ordered the White House to lift access restrictions on The Associated Press, which continued — and continues — to use “Gulf of Mexico” in its news articles. (NOTUS also uses “Gulf of Mexico” in general references.)

Local jurisdictions have also defied Trump. In Florida, for example, Longboat Key leaders voted to keep the town’s “Gulf of Mexico Drive” and not change signage to “Gulf of America Drive.”

In New York, the lone U.S. state that touches Lake Ontario, there are thousands of governmental, commercial and private references to the lake — the world’s 13th-largest by surface area. The word “Ontario” is believed to come from “kanadario,” a word from the Iroquois, whose nations and territories historically spanned much of modern-day New York state and southern Ontario in Canada.

While some people and jurisdictions in New York might feel compelled or cajoled to make a “Lake America” switch, many others may simply choose to ignore Trump’s wishes and maintain their Lake Ontario status quo.

The “Gulf of America” experience also suggests that companies producing widely used maps could come to different conclusions on a “Lake America.” Google Maps, for one, lists “Gulf of America” for users in the United States but “Gulf of Mexico” in Mexico and both names side-by-side elsewhere. National Geographic map products on sale to U.S. customers still display “Gulf of Mexico.”

How Would Foreign Nations Treat ‘Lake America’?

With contempt or dismissiveness, if the past is prologue.

There’s almost zero chance Canada, with hundreds of miles of Lake Ontario shoreline and a province of the same name, would recognize “Lake America” in any formal fashion.

Other nations would also remain effectively free to call Lake Ontario whatever they wanted.

There’s an entity known as the United Nations Group of Experts on Geographical Names that “supports the national and international standardization of geographical names.” But the group has no power to standardize geographic names.

What About Non-Lake Ontarios?

Take Ontario County in New York. Because there’s no federal-level mechanism for changing a county’s name — such a change would be a state- and local-level affair — the largely rural area in the bucolic Finger Lakes region is almost certainly safe.

There’s the city of Ontario, California, near Los Angeles, along with municipal Ontarios in New York, Oregon, Ohio and Wisconsin. Same deal as counties: American presidents have no jurisdiction over municipality names. It’s also exceedingly rare and decidedly inconvenient for local officials to change a city or town name. Signs, schools, buildings, boulevards, parks and most any other place bearing the old moniker would eventually need to change along with it. Still, it’s technically possible: In 1954, for example, Mauch Chunk and East Mauch Chunk in Pennsylvania combined to become the borough of Jim Thorpe, named for the early-20th century athlete and Olympian.

entries.title: Rep. Beatty Says Trump Is Using Mob-Like Tactics in Kennedy Center Battle
entries.summary: “A breathtaking assault on the rule of law,” Rep. Joyce Beatty’s lawyers wrote in a court filing seeking a judicial injunction.
entries.content:
Rep. Joyce Beatty said in a court filing attempting to block changes to the Kennedy Center that the Trump administration is threatening to destroy the fabled performing arts center if it doesn’t get its way.

“In plain English, Defendants have not-so-subtly said: ‘What a nice Kennedy Center you have here. What a shame should something happen to it,’” Beatty’s lawyers wrote in a motion Wednesday. “This is a breathtaking assault on the rule of law. It is delusional. And it must stop.”

Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center’s board of trustees, said in her motion that Trump’s team is misleading the court about the financial losses at the center and, in fact, it’s Trump’s actions that have caused the drop in patronage and donations.

The filing is part of an effort to halt Trump from emblazoning his name on the center, which was blocked by a federal judge. The center’s board, installed with Trump allies, then voted on Aug. 13 to shut down the facility for up to two years to carry out a $250 million renovation project.

The board also voted to inscribe a tribute to the president — "Renovated and Restored by President Donald J. Trump" — on the front of the building and rename the front area as "President Donald J. Trump Plaza." In a court filing Monday, Justice Department lawyers said the changes are necessary to stave off more serious measures that could include demolishing the center.

Beatty’s legal team said Wednesday that Trump’s lawyers “consciously chose to play a dangerous game of chicken with the law. They voted to defy the Court’s decision and restore Donald Trump’s name to the Kennedy Center. They refused to wait for the Court to rule, manufacturing an unnecessary fire drill. And now they have threatened the destruction of the Kennedy Center, a sacred memorial to a fallen President, all in the name of one man’s vanity.”

Beatty’s lawyers also wrote that the Trump administration has not disputed that adding Trump’s name to the building — which was taken off but tarped over from public view — may have “irrevocably damaged the Center’s historic marble facade.”

entries.title: Maryland Judge Strikes Down Democratic Redistricting Ballot Measure
entries.summary: Democrats immediately appealed the ruling to the state Supreme Court.
entries.content:
A Maryland judge on Wednesday blocked a congressional redistricting amendment from appearing on the ballot this November, after state lawmakers voted to add the referendum during a special legislative session this summer.

Maryland joined a wave of Democratic states that launched redistricting efforts in reaction to President Donald Trump’s push for Republicans to flip additional House seats ahead of the midterms. The state’s new map, which would favor Democrats in all eight House districts, would not go into effect until at least 2028.

The Oversight Project, a conservative advocacy group, filed a lawsuit opposing the redistricting effort after Democrats in the state legislature passed an amendment this month to get the measure on the ballot. Democrats appealed the judge’s decision to the Maryland Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon, a spokesperson for Gov. Wes Moore confirmed to NOTUS.

During a July special legislative session, Maryland lawmakers passed a measure that would allow the state to pursue a new redistricting map, clarify the requirements for congressional district boundaries and give the state Supreme Court the sole authority to hear these cases first before the traditional lower-court appeals process.

Anne Arundel County Circuit Judge Robert J. Thompson concluded that the ballot measure is flawed because it would pose multiple redistricting questions to voters.

“The question itself is defective because not only does it ostensibly intend to ‘clarify’ the application of compactness requirements, but it also seeks to confer original jurisdiction over congressional redistricting cases to the Supreme Court of Maryland,” Thompson wrote, adding that the state’s constitution requires a referendum to pose questions about a single issue.

Maryland Democrats’ court loss is another example of a court striking down redistricting efforts from blue states this year. In neighboring Virginia, the state Supreme Court invalidated a similar ballot measure, largely on procedural grounds.

entries.title: A Judge Says Texas Authorities Can Release an ICE Agent Who Shot a Man
entries.summary: Minnesota officials sought to force extradition of the agent to face charges.
entries.content:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who shot a man in Minneapolis could be released from a Texas jail this week despite still being wanted on criminal charges in Minnesota.

On Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. ruled against Minnesota’s attempt to force Texas to turn over Christian Castro, 52, concluding that the state’s lawsuit was filed too soon.

“Based on the current record, the court concludes that it lacks subject matter jurisdiction

because the case is not ripe for adjudication,” Rodriguez, who was appointed to the federal bench by President Donald Trump in 2018, wrote.

Minnesota sued when Texas Gov. Greg Abbott refused to approve what is legally supposed to be “a summary procedure” in which a governor acquiesces to another state’s request to send a defendant to another state to face charges.

However, the judge said that technically Abbott hasn’t said no — he just hasn’t made a decision yet.

“Governor Abbott has not denied the request for a rendition warrant,” Rodriguez wrote. “Minnesota alleges that Governor Abbott has ‘refused to sign’ and has ‘with[eld]’ the rendition warrant. But the record reflects only that Governor Abbott has neither agreed nor refused to sign the rendition warrant as to Castro.”

Texas law only allows the state to jail someone for up to 90 days when that person is a fugitive wanted in another state.

In court, Minnesota had alternatively asked that Cameron County Sheriff Manuel Treviño not release Castro from jail until the Texas governor signed a rendition warrant. However, Rodriguez wrote that “no grounds support a temporary restraining order requiring Sheriff Trevino to ignore the dictates of Texas Code of Criminal Procedure.”

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, who filed the lawsuit, said in a statement that Abbott was “playing with constitutional fire.”

“This case should concern officials and citizens of every state. If a governor can delay extraditions and cherry-pick cases according to their political tastes, then no state will be able to hold fugitive criminals accountable,” Ellison said.

Castro was arrested in May by Texas Rangers who were flanked by investigators with Minnesota’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension. Since then, ICE’s Office of Professional Responsibility has monitored Castro’s jail calls and turned over summaries of those conversations to Minnesota investigators.

Minnesota officials told the judge that Castro has been in communication with a girlfriend in Mexico and plans to reunite with her south of the border. That situation has led Minnesota officials to warn about the possibility that Castro will flee the country.

Abbott’s decision not to abide by Minnesota’s request comes after years of political stunts to draw attention to his hardline anti-immigration stance, including forcibly sending busloads of migrants to liberal sanctuary cities and to then-Vice President Kamala Harris home at the U.S. Naval Observatory in Washington.
